indian-war-canoe

A big carved canoe from the Pacific Northwest Coast, with bold shapes and strong colors. Emily Carr, a painter from Victoria, British Columbia, visited Indigenous villages to record their carvings and canoes. She was one of the first non-Indigenous artists in Canada to take this art seriously. The picture shows her respect for the beauty of what she saw.
community-house-ucluelet

A big wooden community house stands in the village of Ucluelet on the west coast of Vancouver Island. Emily Carr visited the village in 1912 and painted the building with bold, simple shapes. She wanted to record the Indigenous villages that were changing quickly. It's an important historical record as well as a painting.
self-portrait-emily-carr

Emily Carr looks out with a calm, direct gaze, a short-haired woman in a plain jacket. She was one of Canada's greatest painters, a woman who spent much of her life alone with her pet monkey, dogs and her paintbrushes in British Columbia. She wasn't recognized until she was in her fifties, when the Group of Seven discovered her art. This portrait shows her determination.
kitwancool

Tall carved totem poles stand against a dark forest and a sky in a First Nations village in northern British Columbia. Emily Carr visited Kitwancool (Gitanyow) in 1928 and painted the poles with great power and respect. She felt she was recording a culture that deserved to be remembered. It's one of her strongest paintings of the Northwest Coast.
the-indian-church

A small white church stands in the dark forest of Yuquot on Vancouver Island, with a glowing light around it. Emily Carr painted it in her bold, expressive style, and its glowing, simple shape makes it unforgettable. Also called 'Church at Yuquot Village', it shows her gift for combining nature and faith. It's one of the most famous Canadian paintings and hangs in the Art Gallery of Ontario.
akonessen

A portrait of a Huron-Wendat man, painted by Eugène Hamel, a Quebec artist. The Huron-Wendat have lived in the Quebec area for centuries. Painters of the time often recorded the faces of Indigenous people they knew. It's a quiet, dignified portrait.
buffalo-in-combat

Two huge buffalo lock horns in a fierce battle on the open prairie. Frederick Arthur Verner was a Canadian painter who traveled across the Canadian west and painted the buffalo and the plains. He is known for sunset scenes of the buffalo, which he painted often. The picture captures the wild strength of the animals before their herds disappeared.
ojibwa-camp-northern-shore-of-lake-huron

An Ojibwe camp sits on the shore of Lake Huron, with tents and canoes under a wide sky. Frederick Arthur Verner painted Indigenous people and the northern landscape. The scene records a way of life by the Great Lakes. It's an important image of 19th-century Canada.
armistice-day-toronto

A huge crowd with flags and banners packs a Toronto street to celebrate the end of World War I. George Agnew Reid was a Canadian painter who was a leader in Toronto's art world. He painted this on the first Armistice Day in 1918 or 1919. It's a great record of public joy.
forging-6-inch-shells-cluff-ammunition-company-toronto

Factory workers hammer glowing red-hot metal into shells in a busy, smoky factory. George Agnew Reid was commissioned to paint Canada's wartime work, including women and men in factories. The orange glow of the hot metal lights up the dark room. It's a record of the home front in World War I.
l-arrivee-de-champlain-a-quebec

Samuel de Champlain steps off a boat at Quebec in 1608 as he founds the city, while the shoreline is shown behind him. Henri Beau, a Canadian painter, painted this to mark the 300th birthday of Quebec City. It's a scene from the founding of New France. It shows how Canadians remembered their history.
evening-on-the-wharf

People and boats gather on a harbor wharf at dusk, with the glow of sunset. Henry Sandham, a Canadian painter from Montreal, was a master of landscapes and harbor scenes. He later moved to Boston and London. It's a quiet seaside moment.
beacon-light-saint-john-harbour

A lighthouse beams over a harbor at Saint John, New Brunswick, as ships rest in the dark waters. Henry Sandham painted Atlantic Canada's ports and coasts in a clear, careful way. The tiny light in the dark creates a mood of safety. It's a lovely night scene.
a-coming-storm-in-the-adirondacks

Dark storm clouds roll over a mountain valley, with trees swaying in the wind. Homer Watson was a self-taught painter from Ontario, whom Oscar Wilde admired. He painted dramatic skies and landscapes. The painting shows nature's power.
down-in-the-laurentides

Woods and hills spread out in the Laurentian Mountains of Quebec, painted in rich greens and browns. Homer Watson was called Canada's greatest landscape painter of his day. He painted what he saw around him in Ontario and Quebec. It's a calm, natural scene.
a-ravine-farm

A farm sits at the edge of a ravine, with trees and rolling land. Homer Watson, from Doon, Ontario, painted the farms and woods near his home. His quiet, thoughtful pictures became symbols of Canadian landscape. It's a gentle country view.
nut-gatherers-in-the-forest

Children and a woman gather nuts in a forest in autumn, in warm light. Homer Watson was known for his landscapes but occasionally included people. The picture feels peaceful and golden. It's a cozy autumn day.
camp-at-sunrise

A camp in the woods is lit by the first rays of sunrise, with smoke rising from a campfire. Homer Watson painted this late in his career, with softer colors. The warm light is magic. It's a quiet and calm early morning.
labour-aux-premieres-lueurs-du-jour

A farmer with oxen plows a field at dawn, in a misty light that shines on the earth. Horatio Walker, a Canadian painter from Ontario who lived on Île d'Orléans near Quebec City, painted the farmers and animals of rural Quebec. He admired the French painter Millet. It's a noble picture of work on the land.
in-the-shade-of-the-apple-tree

Farm animals rest in the shade of an apple tree on a sunny day. Horatio Walker painted the quiet farm life on Île d'Orléans, where he lived for much of the year. The light and shade are peaceful. It's a warm, country scene.
morning-milking

A farm woman milks a cow in the early morning light of a barnyard. Horatio Walker was known as the painter of Quebec farm life, and he sold many paintings in the United States. The soft light and calm mood are typical of his style. It's a charming rural scene.
blanche-baume

A woman in a stylish dress sits in a gentle, modern style. James Wilson Morrice was a Canadian painter who lived mostly in Paris and was friends with Matisse. He painted with soft, bright colors and simplified shapes. He's now seen as Canada's first great modern painter.
house-in-santiago

A white house with a red roof stands in the sunny Caribbean, painted in a few clean, bright colors. James Wilson Morrice traveled to Cuba and the Caribbean in the winter. His light, simple style was ahead of its time. It's a sun-filled picture.
la-vision-de-saint-roch

A saint kneels in a vision with a dog at his side as angels appear in the sky. Joseph Légaré was one of the first Canadian-born painters, from Quebec City. He copied European paintings and painted religious works for churches. It's an example of early Quebec art.
paysage-au-monument-a-wolfe

A quiet landscape with a monument that honors General Wolfe, who died at the Battle of the Plains of Abraham in 1759. Joseph Légaré painted this in Quebec City, near the site. It is a calm picture with a big history behind it. It's an early Canadian landscape.
l-incendie-du-quartier-saint-jean-a-quebec-vu-vers-l-ou

A huge fire lights up the night sky over Quebec City, with people rushing through the street. Joseph Légaré witnessed the great fire of 1845 in Saint-Jean neighborhood and painted it with powerful color. It's one of Canada's earliest paintings of a disaster. It's a vivid record of the event.
interesting-story

A young girl, with a book in her lap, listens carefully as a story is read to her. Laura Muntz Lyall was a Canadian painter from Toronto who became well known for her paintings of mothers and children. She painted in a soft, delicate style and exhibited in Paris and London. It's a sweet and quiet moment.
miners-houses-glace-bay

Rows of tall, plain houses stand in a coal town in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, with smoke and snow. Lawren Harris, a member of the Group of Seven, painted this in 1925, using strong, simple shapes. He wanted to show the dignity of working people in Canadian life. It's an iconic painting of Canada's industrial past.
shepherdess-at-vallangoujard-seine-et-oise

A young shepherdess stands in a sunny field in France with her sheep. Suzor-Coté, a Quebec painter, studied in Paris and loved the French countryside. He later painted Canadian winter landscapes. It's an early, gentle picture from his time in France.
jacques-cartier-meeting-the-indians-at-stadacona-1535

The French explorer Jacques Cartier meets the people of Stadacona, a village near what is now Quebec City, in 1535. Suzor-Coté painted the encounter as part of Canada's early history. The picture shows the first contact between French explorers and the Iroquoian people. It's a famous scene in Canadian history.
biskra

A town in the Algerian desert, with white buildings and strong sun. Maurice Cullen, a Montreal painter, traveled to North Africa and painted its vivid colors. He is best known for his snowy Canadian winter scenes. It's an unusual desert view by a painter of snow.
camouflaged-nissen-huts

Rows of simple huts painted in camouflage patterns stand in a muddy World War I camp. Maurice Cullen was a Canadian official war artist who went to France in 1918. His paintings record what soldiers' daily lives were like. It's a quiet record of wartime.
dawn-on-the-ouse-trench

A gray dawn light shines over a battlefield, with trenches and bare ground. Maurice Cullen painted this as an official Canadian war artist. The quiet colors seem to show both beauty and sadness. It's a thoughtful war landscape.
ablain-st-nazaire

The ruined village of Ablain-Saint-Nazaire in France sits in rubble after the fighting of World War I. Maurice Cullen painted the ruins after Canadian troops fought near here at Vimy Ridge. The broken buildings show the cost of war. It's a record of a village changed by history.
cite-ste-catherine

A scene of a French town damaged by war, with broken walls and a quiet sky. Maurice Cullen painted the places where Canadian soldiers served in 1918. The painting is quiet and respectful. It's part of a series that preserves the memory of the war.
fort-edmonton

A wooden fort sits on a hill above the North Saskatchewan River, with tents and people at its base. Paul Kane traveled across Canada in 1846–48, sketching the fur trade posts and the Indigenous peoples he met. Fort Edmonton was a major hub of the fur trade. It's an early picture of what is now a big city.
a-woman-weaving-a-blanket

An Indigenous woman sits and weaves a blanket from wool on a simple loom. Paul Kane traveled to the Pacific coast and painted Indigenous crafts and daily life. His pictures help us see how people lived in the 1840s. It's a record of skill and tradition.
freeman-schermerhorn-clench

A man in formal dress sits for a portrait in a calm pose. Paul Kane was a portrait painter before he made his famous journey across Canada. This early work shows his training. It's part of the story of how Kane became an artist.
eliza-clarke-cory-clench

A woman in a bonnet and a plain dress sits for her portrait. Paul Kane painted portraits in Ontario before his great journey to the west. The carefully painted face shows his skill. It's an early Canadian portrait.
scene-in-the-northwest-portrait-of-john-henry-lefroy

A British officer and scientist, John Henry Lefroy, stands in a winter landscape in the Canadian northwest, dressed in a warm fur coat, with sled dogs. Paul Kane met him on his trip across Canada. Lefroy was studying the earth's magnetism. It's a famous Canadian portrait of the fur trade era.
flathead-woman-with-child

An Indigenous mother holds her baby in a cradleboard. Paul Kane painted this on the Pacific coast, recording how the baby's head was shaped as part of a custom. His paintings are valuable records of the customs of many peoples. It's a gentle family portrait.
assiniboine-hunting-buffalo

Assiniboine hunters on horseback race across the plains, chasing a herd of buffalo. Paul Kane painted this on his trip across the prairies in the 1840s. The galloping horses and flying dust are full of excitement. It's one of the most famous Canadian paintings of the plains.
chinook-indians-in-front-of-mount-hood

Chinook people stand in front of a huge snowy volcano, Mount Hood, on the Columbia River. Paul Kane painted this on his journey to the Pacific Northwest. The mountain towers over the scene. It's a grand landscape of a faraway place.
mother-love

A mother cuddles her baby in a loving embrace, with a warm and tender mood. Paul Peel was a Canadian painter from London, Ontario, who became a star in Paris. He is known for tender pictures of mothers and children. It's a sweet, gentle family picture.
japanese-dolls-and-fan

Colorful Japanese dolls and a fan are laid out together, with a bright patterned cloth. Paul Peel loved to paint beautiful objects, and Japanese goods were popular in Paris. The bright colors and rich textures are charming. It's a lovely still life.
the-young-botanist

A young girl in a long dress leans over to study a flower, in a sunlit garden. Paul Peel painted children with great charm. The picture won him a medal at the Paris Salon. It's one of Canada's best-known paintings of childhood.
bedtime

Two little children in nightclothes kneel to say their prayers beside a warm fire. Paul Peel was famous in Paris for his scenes of cozy childhood. The glow of the firelight is lovely. It's a charming picture of bedtime.
the-young-shepherdess-paul-peel
A young barefoot girl stands in a sunlit field with her sheep. Paul Peel painted country children in soft light. The peaceful scene was popular in Paris. It's a sweet pastoral picture.
fathers-of-confederation

A group of men stand and sit in a conference room in Quebec City in 1864, planning a new country: Canada. The painter Robert Harris created it long after the meeting, and it shows 33 delegates gathered at the Quebec Conference. It became a symbol of the birth of Canada. The original burned in a fire in 1916, and this is a copy of the lost painting.
john-7th-earl-of-aberdeen-later-1st-marquess-montreal

A distinguished gentleman in formal dress sits in a stately pose. Robert Harris, who was born in Wales and grew up in Prince Edward Island, was one of Canada's top portrait painters. The Earl of Aberdeen was a governor general of Canada. It's a formal portrait of a public figure.
